blocks.text: **Insertion sort** sorts the way you arrange playing cards in your hand: keep the cards you've already picked up in order, and slide each new card left until it sits in the right place. The front of the array is always sorted, and it grows by one value each step.

blocks.alt: Inserting 6 into the sorted prefix 5, 11, 12. The values 12 and 11 are bigger than 6, so each shifts one place right, and 6 drops into the gap after 5. The prefix becomes 5, 6, 11, 12.

elements.text: shift bigger values right, then drop the new value into the gap
elements.originalText: shift bigger values right, then drop the new value into the gap

items: Treat `nums[0]` as a sorted prefix of length 1.
Take the next value, the **key**. Walk left through the sorted prefix: while a value is bigger than the key, shift it one place right.
When you meet a value that isn't bigger (or reach the front), drop the key into the gap. The sorted prefix is now one longer. Repeat until the end.

blocks.caption: Each key is taken out, bigger values shift right, and the key drops into the gap.

blocks.text: The work is the number of shifts, which equals the number of **inversions** — pairs that are in the wrong order. A reversed array has n(n − 1)/2 of them: **O(n²)**. A sorted array has none, and each key is checked once: **O(n)**. A nearly sorted array, with each value only a few places from home, is close to O(n). Extra space is **O(1)**.

blocks.alt: Best: already sorted: O(n) time, O(1) space. Average and worst: O(n²) time, O(1) space.

items: **Stable** — the shift loop stops at the first value that's not bigger, so equal values keep their order.
**Adaptive** — the fewer inversions, the faster it runs.
**Online** — it can sort values as they arrive, one at a time.

blocks.text: For **small** arrays (up to a few dozen values) and **nearly sorted** ones it beats the O(n log n) sorts, because its inner loop is so simple. That's why real libraries use it inside their fast sorts: Python's and Java's Timsort and C++'s introsort switch to insertion sort for short runs.

items: Grow a **sorted prefix**; shift bigger values right and drop each new key into the gap.
**O(n²)** worst case, **O(n)** on sorted input; **O(1)** space; **stable** and **adaptive**.
The best simple sort — and part of the built-in sorts you use every day.
